British Journal of Educational Technolog.title:
Generative
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    empowered contextual educational games as facilitators of elementary school students' computational thinking tendencies
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    
                    Computational thinking (CT) is a critical skill for the 21st century. To enhance students' engagement in CT‐related learning activities, educational games are considered an effective tool, especially for younger students. However, the absence of individualized feedback may limit their potential. To address this challenge, a generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)‐empowered contextual gaming environment was developed. A quasi‐experimental study was conducted with two intact fifth‐grade classes at an elementary school in eastern China. After controlling for pretest scores, the experimental group showed a modest but statistically significant advantage in self‐reported CT tendencies compared with the control group, whereas no significant between‐group difference was found in algorithmic knowledge. Students in the experimental group valued the opportunity to ask questions of GenAI‐powered non‐player characters (NPCs). The qualitative findings suggest that GenAI primarily functioned as motivational and cognitive scaffolding by encouraging inquiry, supporting problem clarification and sustaining engagement, rather than as a direct mechanism for improving algorithmic knowledge during the short intervention. These findings should be interpreted cautiously because CT tendencies were measured through self‐report, the intervention lasted 3 instructional weeks, and the sample was drawn from a single school. The study therefore provides preliminary evidence regarding the potential of GenAI‐supported contextual games to foster CT‐related tendencies and inquiry behaviours among elementary school students.
                  
                  
                    
                    
                      
                        
                          Practitioner notes
                        
                        
                          What is already known about this topic
                          
                            
                              Game‐based learning (GBL) has been shown to support student development, particularly in enhancing primary school students' CT‐related tendencies and problem‐solving orientations.
                            
                            
                              Generative AI (GenAI) has the potential to support personalized learning support within a GBL environment to facilitate learning.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          What this paper adds
                          
                            
                              After adjustment for pretest scores, students in the GenAI‐enhanced condition showed a modest but statistically significant advantage in self‐reported CT tendencies compared with those in the conventional GBL condition.
                            
                            
                              Interaction with GenAI‐powered NPCs in a GBL environment can stimulate students' inquiry, engagement and problem‐solving awareness.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          Implications for practice and/or policy:
                          
                            
                              This study highlights the importance of engaging students in exploration, dialogue, reflection and repeated practice for fostering CT tendencies.
                            
                            
                              Role‐playing contextual educational games, when integrated with GenAI, can effectively nurture students' CT tendencies while sustaining their motivation and engagement.

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title:
Human tutoring, generative
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    tutoring and independent internet search: A randomised between‐subjects experiment on students' responses to academic challenge
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly available as a source of interactive academic support, raising questions about how it shapes learning. Research has focused on performance outcomes, with less attention to learners' behavioural and affective responses to academic challenge, even though productive engagement with challenge supports deeper learning. In this randomised between‐subjects experiment, students aged 16–18 at an English sixth‐form college worked on two sections of challenging mathematics questions with one of three forms of support: one‐to‐one human tutoring, a GenAI tutor or unguided internet search. Measures included self‐reported effort and perceived difficulty, questions attempted, post‐task stress and subsequent challenge‐seeking. Support condition was associated with different response patterns. Students using the GenAI tutor reported higher effort and perceived difficulty than those receiving human tutoring by the second section. Descriptively, post‐task responses showed a lower proportion of stressed responses under GenAI tutoring than internet search. Human tutoring showed the lowest perceived difficulty and highest number of attempts in both sections, although significant pairwise differences varied by section. It also showed descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses. Challenge‐seeking did not differ by condition and was instead strongly associated with trait challenge‐seeking. The findings suggest that the GenAI tutor used in this study offered a form of support distinct from both human tutoring and unguided internet search, with potential value during independent practice rather than as a replacement for human teaching. They demonstrate the importance of evaluating AI‐supported learning beyond performance outcomes and through behavioural and affective responses to difficulty.
                  
                    
                      
                        Practitioner notes
                      
                      
                        What is already known about this topic
                        
                          
                            Productive struggle with challenging tasks is important for learning, but its benefits depend on how learners respond when difficulty is encountered.
                          
                          
                            Human tutors can support productive responses to challenge through scaffolding and co‐regulation, helping learners manage effort, difficulty and emotional responses.
                          
                          
                            Generative AI tools are increasingly used by students during independent study, but much existing research has focused on performance outcomes rather than learning processes or learner behaviour.
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        What this paper adds
                        
                          
                            This study provides experimental evidence comparing a human tutor, a generative AI tutor and independent internet search in how students respond behaviourally and affectively to academic challenge.
                          
                          
                            Working with the GenAI tutor was associated with higher reported effort than human tutoring in the second task section, alongside higher perceived difficulty. Post‐task responses also showed a descriptively lower proportion of stressed responses than under unguided internet search.
                          
                          
                            By contrast, human tutoring was associated with the highest number of attempts in both sections, lower perceived difficulty and descriptively the lowest proportion of stressed responses, indicating a distinct and more supportive role when students encounter difficulty.
                          
                          
                            Findings suggest that different forms of support may shape how students experience and work through challenge, while subsequent challenge‐seeking was more closely associated with students' pre‐existing dispositions.
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        Implications for practice and/or policy
                        
                          
                            Support choices shape learners' engagement with difficulty and should therefore be treated as pedagogical decisions rather than neutral sources of help.
                          
                          
                            The pattern observed with Khanmigo Lite suggests that GenAI tutor support may help sustain engagement during challenging academic work without resolving difficulty.
                          
                          
                            The GenAI tutor examined here may offer a more supportive alternative to unguided internet search during independent practice, although designs and capabilities vary and evolve. Such tools should supplement rather than replace human teaching, with educators supporting learning and addressing unresolved difficulty.
                          
                          
                            Evaluations of AI‐supported learning should attend to learners' behavioural and affective responses to challenge, rather than focusing solely on end products or task completion.

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title:
The impact of an
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    ‐driven multimodal teaching analytics dashboard on pre‐service teachers' reflective learning in microteaching
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Microteaching is a cornerstone of teacher education, enabling pre‐service teachers (PSTs) to rehearse, observe and refine instructional practices through structured reflection. Traditional video‐based review in microteaching is often time‐consuming and insufficiently analytical. Although learning analytics dashboards (LADs) can visualize teaching data to support reflection, many remain descriptive, offering limited insight into how behavioural evidence relates to pedagogical meaning. To address this gap, this study introduces iTeachBoard, an AI‐driven multimodal teaching analytics dashboard that integrates layered multimodal timeline visualization based on data‐storytelling design principle with LLM‐generated narrative feedback to support reflective learning in microteaching. A quasi‐experimental study (
                    n
                     = 53) compared iTeachBoard with a conventional visual analytics dashboard (VAD). Results revealed that iTeachBoard significantly enhanced PSTs' data interpretation, meaning construction and reflective writing depth. Participants perceived narrative‐style feedback as more trustworthy, explainable and pedagogically relevant. These findings suggest that LLM‐driven multimodal learning analytics can help bridge data visualization and pedagogical interpretation, thereby supporting PSTs' sense‐making, particularly data interpretation and meaning construction, as well as reflective writing depth in microteaching.
                  
                  
                    
                      
                        Practitioner notes
                      
                      
                        What is already known about this topic
                        
                          
                            Microteaching offers pre‐service teachers (PSTs) valuable opportunities to rehearse lessons, receive feedback and reflect on their teaching. However, reflections often remain superficial due to limited feedback structure and lack of actionable guidance.
                          
                          
                            Learning analytics dashboards (LADs) can visualize teaching behaviours, but most rely on descriptive metrics that lack interpretability and pedagogical relevance.
                          
                          
                            Sense‐making and data‐storytelling design principles have been proposed to help PSTs connect learning data with pedagogical meaning, yet empirical validation in teacher education remains scarce.
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        What this paper adds
                        
                          
                            Introduces iTeachBoard, an AI‐driven multimodal LAD that integrates large language model (LLM)‐based narrative feedback with multimodal visualizations to support deep reflective learning in microteaching.
                          
                          
                            Proposes the AI for Microteaching Multimodal Analytics Model (AI4MT), linking observable teaching behaviours to pedagogically meaningful reflective dimensions.
                          
                          
                            Provides empirical evidence that narrative‐style feedback combined with multimodal visualization significantly improves PSTs' overall sense‐making, with significant gains in data interpretation and meaning construction, as well as reflective writing depth, compared with a conventional video analytics dashboard.
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        Implications for practice and/or policy
                        
                          
                            iTeachBoard can be implemented in teacher education and professional development to promote evidence‐based reflection, collaborative lesson analysis and continuous pedagogical improvement.
                          
                          
                            The dashboard can enhance teachers' data literacy and AI literacy, fostering meaningful engagement with multimodal feedback for reflective growth.
                          
                          
                            Institutions should develop policies ensuring ethical data use, privacy protection and transparency in AI‐supported reflective systems to promote responsible adoption in educational settings.

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title:
<scp>GenAI</scp>
                    ‐based metacognitive prompting in collaborative inquiry: A comparison across diverse preconception groups
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    
                    Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into collaborative inquiry to provide metacognitive prompting that scaffolds socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL). Understanding how such GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting is taken up through student–GenAI interactions is therefore critical. However, although learner–GenAI interaction processes have been widely examined, little is known about how learners' preconceptions shape their engagement with GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting. This study examined how groups with different or similar preconceptions about energy forms and conservation differed in their engagement with GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting during collaborative inquiry. Participants comprised 14 small groups, including eight groups with different preconceptions (D groups) and six groups with similar preconceptions (S groups). The distribution of learner‐generated inquiries directed to the written metacognitive AI (MAI) was largely comparable across groups. Lag sequential analysis revealed contrasting patterns in how groups evaluated the metacognitive prompts: D groups showed sustained positive or neutral evaluation of the prompts, whereas S groups showed sustained negative evaluation. Process mining further showed that AI query negotiation served as a hub in D groups' collaboration, connecting their conceptual discussions and task coordination. In S groups, by contrast, it formed part of a simpler, linear sequence of querying the AI and processing its responses. This study advances understanding of how preconception diversity shapes the processes and dynamics of human–AI collaboration. The findings show that AI‐mediated regulation varies depending on group‐level knowledge configurations.
                  
                  
                    
                    
                      
                        
                          Practitioner notes
                        
                        
                          What is already known about this topic
                          
                            
                              Effective collaborative inquiry depends on learners' prior knowledge resources and their regulatory capacity.
                            
                            
                              Preconceptions, as a core component of prior knowledge, shape how learners interpret problems and engage in conceptual discussion.
                            
                            
                              GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting is designed to externalise metacognitive awareness and scaffold learners' regulatory processes.
                            
                            
                              Regulation unfolds through temporally ordered interaction sequences that reveal underlying regulatory dynamics.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          What this paper adds
                          
                            
                              This study compares how different preconception groups and similar preconception groups engage with GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting during collaborative scientific inquiry.
                            
                            
                              GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting responded to similar types of learner inquiries across groups.
                            
                            
                              GenAI query interaction in different preconception groups appeared more integrated with conceptual and task discussion, whereas in similar preconception groups it followed a more linear, output‐focused path.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          Implications for practice and/or policy
                          
                            
                              GenAI‐based metacognitive prompting may benefit from incorporating a preliminary classification layer that distinguishes between metacognitive prompts and procedural or informational requests.
                            
                            
                              Teachers may consider preconception diversity when forming groups, as different epistemic configurations appear to give rise to distinct patterns of GenAI‐learner collaboration.
                            
                            
                              Policymakers and designers should recognise that GenAI functions as a co‐regulator within collaborative settings, and its impact depends on how it is interactionally integrated into group interactional trajectories.

Educational Technology Research and Deve.title: Developing and validating the human-AI collaboration competency scale
Educational Technology Research and Deve.abstract:
Abstract
                  Fostering learners’ capacity to collaborate effectively with AI has become an important goal in education. This study aims to develop and validate the Human–AI Collaboration Competency (HACC) Scale, which can be used to assess students’ perceived competency in allocating roles and managing tasks, and sharing, coordinating, and integrating with AI through ongoing interaction to achieve a common goal. This scale includes five constructs’’: engagement, fluency, team bond, interdependence, and task regulation. Two independent samples of high school students were used to examine the factor structures: Sample 1 (n = 195) was used for exploratory factor analysis (EFA), and Sample 2 (n = 356) was used for confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). The final version of the HACC Scale consisted of 25 items loaded onto 5 factors. Construct validity was supported through EFA and CFA, and evidence for convergent validity was obtained by examining the correlations between the measures of digital literacy, AI literacy, AI attitude, and collaborative learning skills. The findings provide empirical support for the internal structure and external associations of the HACC Scale, showing that this scale provides a basis for future research and instructional practices aimed at enhancing human–AI collaboration.

Educational Technology Research and Deve.title: Proposing a culturally relevant theoretical framework for teacher educators’ information and communication technology (ICT) acceptance and use in Bhutan and similar cultural contexts
Educational Technology Research and Deve.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Technology acceptance by teacher educators is crucial for successful integration into teaching. While technology acceptance models are well established in developed-country contexts, comparatively little attention has been given to developing models that account for the specific conditions of developing countries and distinct cultural contexts. A convergent mixed-methods approach was employed in Bhutan to investigate the factors that facilitate or hinder ICT acceptance and use in teaching, utilizing an adapted version of the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) model. Data were collected through interviews and surveys. The survey was administered to 90 teacher educators, while semi-structured interviews were conducted with 21 teacher educators teaching in teacher education colleges in Bhutan. The quantitative survey data were analysed using descriptive statistics, while the qualitative interview data were analysed using thematic analysis. The findings revealed that the enabling factors were performance expectancy, social influence, attitude, ICT usage, and Bhutanese cultural values such as
                    gyelkhap lu tha dam tshig
                    (loyalty, dedication, and commitment of a person to the nation), interdependent collective culture which resembles
                    tenchingdrelwa
                    (the idea that all living beings are connected through lives and time) and
                    zhenphen (
                    Buddhist value of selfless intent and action to help each other). The constraints faced included effort expectancy, facilitating conditions and system rigidity due to prescribed curriculum, power distance and mandatory ICT use. Based on these factors, a culturally relevant theoretical framework of teacher educators’ ICT acceptance and use in Bhutan and similar cultural contexts was proposed to maximise ICT uptake in teaching.

Educational Technology Research and Deve.title: The design and impacts of collaborative learning analytics dashboards: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Educational Technology Research and Deve.abstract:
Abstract
                  Collaborative learning analytics dashboards (CLADs), which present visualization-based feedback on collaborative learning processes, offer teachers and students a critical tool for data-informed reflection and decision-making. Previous reviews of learning analytics dashboards have focused on their impact on students’ performance, without specifically considering the design and effectiveness of the dashboards in collaborative learning contexts. The present study fills this gap by providing a systematic review and meta-analysis of the design, implementation, application, and effectiveness of CLADs, based on 51 studies identified using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. We found that teacher-facing CLADs are designed to monitor collaborative learning processes, diagnose collaborative learning difficulties, serve as intervention tools, and support feedback development. In contrast, student-facing CLADs are designed to enhance collaborative interaction, support shared regulation, and increase group awareness. Descriptive analysis was the primary method used to analyse process data in CLADs. A few studies drew on theories to guide the selection of analytical indicators and system development. Our meta-analysis revealed that CLADs have a statistically significant positive effect on student learning performance in collaborative settings. Based on these findings, this study proposes a framework of six interconnected steps that structure the development process of CLADs. The framework provides actionable guidance for developing CLADs that are pedagogically and theoretically grounded, and adaptable to evolving analytical methods.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title:
Examining the Effects of Motivating Language and Personalization in
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    Voice‐Over Educational Videos: From a Social‐Psychological Perspective
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    The development of AI technology is transforming the production of videos. In particular, voice‐over video lectures can be easily produced with AI voice, which has been found to generate learning comparable to that of human voice. Further, verbal cues, which are social cues—critical factors impacting video‐based learning—expressed with words, can be readily implemented with AI voice. However, the influence of verbal cues in video lectures has been relatively underinvestigated, limiting the optimization of (AI) voice‐over educational videos.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    This study aims to explore the effects of motivating language and personalization, both of which are verbal cues—a common but underexplored type of social cues, on learning satisfaction, actual learning outcomes, perceived learning, and rapport in AI voice‐over video lectures.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    A three (motivating language: autonomy‐supportive vs. controlling vs. neutral) × two (personalization: personalized vs. nonpersonalized) between‐subjects experiment was carried out among 182 university students.
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusions
                    Motivating language impacted learning satisfaction, retention, perceived learning, and rapport, and the impacts on learning satisfaction and rapport varied with personalization; but collectively, autonomy‐supportive language was more effective than neutral language, whereas controlling language was ineffective, irrespective of personalization; besides, personalization showed benefits only under autonomy‐supportive language in rapport, and instead caused decreased learning satisfaction and rapport under neutral language. The findings have several theoretical implications, including deepening knowledge about verbal cues, extending theories about effects of social cues in multimedia learning, and broadening understanding of motivating teaching. Practical implications for the design of AI voice‐over video lectures were discussed.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title: Social Participatory Role Enactment in Asynchronous Discussion and Mobile Instant Messaging
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Computer‐supported collaborative learning (CSCL) is widely used in higher education, yet participation remains uneven and discourse often stays at a low cognitive level. Asynchronous online discussion (AOD) and mobile instant messaging (MIM) are two common communication environments, but how social participatory roles are expressed through discourse across these environments remains unclear.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    This study examined conversational‐function and cognitive‐engagement profiles associated with social participatory roles in recorded AOD and MIM interactions.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    Thirty first‐year undergraduates in eight groups completed two collaborative tasks using Blackboard forums (AOD) and Lark (MIM) in a counterbalanced cross‐over design. Social participatory roles were inferred via social network analysis; conversational functions were coded with the ASIMeC‐F scheme; and cognitive engagement was coded at four levels (operation, way‐finding, sense‐making, innovation). Data were analysed using paired role‐distribution comparisons, binary mixed‐effects logistic regression, descriptive role‐specific summaries, and epistemic network analysis (ENA).
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusions
                    No difference in marginal role distributions was detected, although individual role transitions were common. Adjusted models associated AOD with a higher prevalence of Analysing and MIM with a higher prevalence of Respond and Commenting without elaboration. Role‐specific profiles illustrated different discourse patterns under similar role labels, while ENA described co‐occurrence patterns within the conversational‐function and cognitive‐engagement coding schemes. These findings inform a context‐sensitive account of role enactment and suggest role‐based scaffolding for further testing.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title:
Research Trends of Artificial Intelligence‐Facilitated Computational Thinking in K‐12
                    <scp>STEM</scp>
                    : A Systematic Review Through the Lens of Activity Theory
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), research in the cross‐disciplinary field of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education has increasingly focused on how to leverage AI to foster computational thinking (CT) among K‐12 students, given that CT, recognized as a core 21st‐century competency, plays a pivotal role in cultivating students’ literacy and equipping them with the ability to tackle complex problems.
                  
                  
                    Objective
                    Grounded in activity theory, this study seeks to identify the key factors shaping K‐12 students’ CT development in AI‐enhanced STEM education. It systematically analyzes: (a) the subjects involved and the types and roles of AI tools employed, (b) the purposes, periods, and CT dimensions within the object, (c) the methods, strategies, and evaluation performance applied within rules, (d) the learning domains within communities and the interactions within the division of labor, and (e) the developmental trends in outcomes.
                  
                  
                    Method
                    This study employed the PRISMA framework to systematically review 57 SSCI journal publications published between 2017 and 2025. In addition, Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) was utilized to examine the current state of CT evaluation.
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusions
                    Findings indicate that: (1) the primary subjects of the studies were elementary school students; expert systems and robotics were the most prevalent types of AI, which were frequently employed as learning tools; (2) the primary objective was to evaluate the effectiveness of AI in CT–K12–STEM, with periods typically ranging from 2 to 6 months, focusing on conceptual knowledge and practical skills; (3) the rules focused on exploratory learning and gamification strategies, employing quantitative research methods; (4) communities spanned cross‐disciplinary domains, with division of labor tending towards mixed interaction types; and (5) outcomes focused on the learning cognitive perspective, encompassing aspects such as learning performance and problem solving. Based on the research results, practical recommendations are provided for educational researchers and policymakers.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title: Enhancing Learning Performance in Primary School Students Through Real‐Time Versus Delayed Rewards During Pair Inquiry‐Based Visual Programming
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Visual programming has experienced a remarkable surge in popularity recently. Real‐time and delayed rewards are two important incentive mechanisms in designing effective learning activities. However, the examination of their effects on students' learning performance remains limited. Additionally, the comparative analysis of these reward mechanisms in the context of learning visual programming has received insufficient attention.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    We aimed to address this research gap.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    
                      A quasi‐experimental study was conducted involving two classes. One class (
                      n
                       = 32) received real‐time rewards, while the other class (
                      n
                       = 40) received delayed rewards. The study employed independent samples
                      t
                      ‐tests to assess the effects of real‐time versus delayed rewards on students' learning performance and to identify differences between the groups. Additionally, semi‐structured interviews were conducted to gain insights into the underlying reasons behind the findings.
                    
                  
                  
                    Results
                    The results showed that students in the real‐time reward group generally outperformed their counterparts in terms of intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, flow experience and algorithmic thinking. However, only the differences in extrinsic motivation and algorithmic thinking were statistically significant.
                  
                  
                    Conclusions
                    The implications of this study are valuable for educators and researchers, providing insights into how to design and implement visual programming learning activities using diverse reward systems as incentive mechanisms. These findings can help enhance students' learning performance more efficiently.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Comparing AI-Assisted 2D and 3D Block-Based Games for Computational Thinking Development in Introductory Programming
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract:
Computational thinking (CT) is a foundational competency in undergraduate education, yet novice programmers frequently encounter high cognitive demands and declining motivation. Although block-based programming and AI-assisted scaffolding can reduce extraneous load by enabling natural-language interaction, it remains unclear whether embedding these capabilities within immersive three-dimensional environments further enhances CT development through reduced extraneous load and enriched spatial context for schema formation. This study employed a randomized between-subjects design to compare an AI-assisted 3D block-based game (CT Logic 3D) with an AI-assisted 2D counterpart (CT Logic 2D) over a four-week intervention involving fifty undergraduate students (
                    n
                    = 50, Mage = 23.3, SD = 1.07). Both conditions shared identical AI translation pipelines and instructional sequences, with spatial dimensionality constituting the sole experimental manipulation. Results indicated that participants in the 3D condition achieved significantly greater gains in CT (
                    d
                    = 0.54), stronger delayed retention (
                    d
                    = 0.74), and higher near-transfer problem-solving performance (
                    d
                    = 0.82). Relative to the 2D group, participants in the 3D condition completed tasks 22% faster (
                    d
                    = 1.08), reported lower perceived difficulty (
                    d
                    = 0.94), and experienced higher levels of flow (
                    d
                    = 0.89) and intrinsic motivation (
                    d
                    = 0.86). Engagement increased throughout the intervention, with the largest efficiency gains observed among absolute novices. Moreover, substantial rates of learner-initiated modification of AI-generated solutions (3D: 76%; 2D: 71%) indicated active rather than passive use of AI scaffolding. Interpreted through Cognitive Load Theory, the findings suggest that combining AI scaffolding with immersive spatial representations produces measurable advantages for CT development beyond those achievable through AI scaffolding alone. Theoretical and practical implications for the design of AI-enhanced CT instruction are discussed.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Developing and Validating an AI-Literacy-Integrated Teaching Acceptance and Readiness Scale for Mathematics Teachers
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract:
The global shift toward cultivating students’ AI literacy requires teachers to reconceptualize curricula and pedagogical practices. However, research has focused primarily on teachers’ use of AI tools, overlooking their readiness to integrate AI literacy as a learning goal, particularly in mathematics education. In response, this study developed and validated the AI-Literacy-Integrated Teaching Acceptance and Readiness Scale for Mathematics Teachers (AILTAR-M). The instrument was theoretically organized around two domains: (1)
                    Acceptance
                    , comprising four constructs adapted from the Technology Acceptance Model (Perceived Usefulness, Perceived Ease of Use, Attitude toward Use, and Behavioral Intention); and (2)
                    Readiness
                    , encompassing Perceived AI Literacy as a self-reported cognitive dimension and Teaching Self-Efficacy as a motivational dimension. Psychometric evaluation with 549 mathematics teachers in China supported a 29-item, six-factor structure. Exploratory factor analysis (
                    n
                    = 174) yielded a six-factor solution explaining 69.7% of the variance, and confirmatory factor analysis (
                    n
                    = 375) demonstrated acceptable model fit (CFI = .938, TLI = .931, RMSEA = .063, SRMR = .038). The instrument exhibited strong internal consistency (α = .899– .943) alongside satisfactory convergent and discriminant validity. These findings provide initial psychometric evidence for using the AILTAR-M to examine mathematics teachers’ acceptance of and readiness for integrating AI literacy into mathematics instruction.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Design and Evaluation of an Immersive VR Space Based on Pedagogical Agent for Theory of Mind Training in Autistic Children: Insights from Brain Activity and Participatory Study
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract: While virtual reality (VR) offers potential for training children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), limited evidence guides pedagogical agent (PA) design for immersive theory of mind (ToM) training. This study adopted a sequential multi-method approach to develop and preliminarily evaluate a cave automatic virtual environment (CAVE)-based ToM training space for autistic children. Study 1 used functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) with 22 autistic children and found that rich interaction elicited greater neural activation during ToM processing, particularly when anthropomorphic cues were limited. Building on these findings, Study 2 combined interviews with 6 autism education experts and a collage workshop with 8 autistic children. The integrated findings supported cartoon-style human agents with moderate facial expressions, low-saturation and limited colors, diverse movements, expressive speech, simple verbal expressions, stepwise cues, and contingent feedback. These strategies guided development of the CAVE-based training space in Study 3. The preliminary feasibility evaluation indicated satisfactory professional-user usability, with the three participating children showing higher post-training ToM scores and caregiver-reported changes in social functioning. Overall, the study provides design and methodological guidance for immersive learning environments that better align with autistic children’s processing characteristics and intervention needs, while suggesting the potential of the CAVE-based environment for ToM training.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Unraveling the Effects of Block-Based Visual Programming on Students’ Computational Thinking
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract:
Nowadays, computational thinking has been the core necessary skill for students who want to succeed in the 21
                    st
                    century. Block-based visual programming (BBVP) is one of the most widely used ways to develop student computational thinking. However, its impact on student computational thinking is mixed in the education field. This study conducts a meta-analysis to compare the impacts of BBVP and textual programming on student computational thinking. The result covering 24 independent studies and 2,441 students indicates that BBVP has a large positive effect (
                    SMD
                    = 0.887,
                    CI
                    = [0.625, 1.148],
                    p
                    < 0.001) on student computational thinking. We also conduct moderator analysis and find that class size, treatment duration, test type, BBVP type, subject, learning method, and region significantly moderate BBVP’s impacts on students computational thinking. Finally, major findings, recommendations, and limitations are provided.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Toward an Interpretive Synthesis of Personalization, Co-Design, and Ethical Mediation in AI-Supported Higher Education: An Integrative Review of Agentic, Generative, and Adaptive Tutoring Systems
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) and adaptive learning technologies are expanding in higher education, raising questions about their alignment with pedagogical goals. This qualitative-integrative review synthesizes 57 publications (21 empirical, 25 conceptual or framework, 9 systematic reviews or meta-analyses retained for triangulation, and 2 design/development papers) from 2024 to 2026, employing Whittemore and Knafl’s methodology to examine AI-supported tutoring, implementation strategies, and learner/instructor experiences. Three interpretive themes organize this heterogeneous evidence: (1) personalization as a recurring target, from micro-level adaptation to curriculum design; (2) technology-pedagogy co-design as a recurring implementation pattern; and (3) contextual and ethical conditions surrounding adoption, including culture, policy gaps, well-being, and academic integrity. These themes are interpretive, not a validated framework, and draw on evidence of uneven strength. The present review does not estimate effect sizes or pool outcomes across studies; g = 0.70, reported by X. Wang et al. in a separate meta-analysis of 45 studies (2010–2022) of pre-generative adaptive systems, which is cited only as background, not as a finding of this review. Implications are framed as evidence-tiered hypotheses, while the layered model is offered as an interpretive scaffold for future research, not a confirmatory model.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: What counts as digital play? Irish early childhood educators’ beliefs and practice tensions
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Digital technologies are increasingly embedded in young children’s lives, yet uncertainty remains regarding their role in early childhood education and care (ECEC). This study explores Irish early years educators’ beliefs and perceptions concerning digital play, employing Bronfenbrenner’s bioecological framework to examine how policy, parental expectations and professional identity interact to shape children’s learning opportunities. Semi-structured interviews with 10 educators identified five themes: developmentalist beliefs prioritising ‘natural’ play, cautious openness to digital tools, professional identity and ethical tensions, perceptions of children and families and concerns about policy directives. Findings reveal a persistent policy–practice gap, where limited professional development and unclear guidance leave educators uncertain about how to define and implement quality digital play. The study emphasises that educators’ attitudes are closely associated with the extent and quality of children’s digital engagement, highlighting the need for sustained professional development and strengthened mesosystemic communication across home, school and policy contexts. Implications include the creation of context-sensitive frameworks that integrate digital and traditional play while supporting children’s holistic development. This study demonstrates that educators’ definitions of digital play are shaped by the interaction of professional identity, policy ambiguity, family expectations and resource conditions, offering new insight into the conditions that constrain digital play in Irish early years settings.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Teachers’ professional learning and development experiences in Chinese kindergartens: Opportunities and tensions
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Professional learning and development (PLD) activities for Chinese kindergarten teachers have introduced imported knowledge to promote teaching and learning. Much PLD provision is led by leaders and experts rather than teachers. To understand the educational beliefs and power differences that surface among teachers, leaders and experts during PLD sessions and how teachers navigate this complex terrain, this paper presents a post-intentional phenomenological study involving seven participants from two Chinese early childhood settings. Data collection included semi-structured interviews, observations of PLD meetings and videos of teachers’ implementation of PLD ideas. Educational policies, PLD materials, and the researcher’s reflexive journal were also used for analysis. Analysis involved a line-by-line reading process where theoretical concepts, data and researcher reflexivity interacted. The findings reveal that teachers experienced tensions in relation to formal PLD sessions. These tensions stemmed from established values and hierarchical constraints that limited their joint reflection and actions. Our analysis, framed by the concepts of relational agency and in-between spaces, shows how teachers navigated these tensions. Despite these constraints, the teachers responded by creating opportunities for collaborative learning. They sought out informal situations where they had the flexibility to develop shared knowledge. We argue that Chinese teachers’ PLD can occur within and across such tensions and opportunities. These informal situations empowered teachers to enact relational agency by aligning their expertise to make PLD decisions. This process eased tensions and created space for collaborative learning. The study concludes that valuing these informal, teacher-initiated spaces is crucial for moving beyond top-down knowledge transmission and fostering sustainable professional growth in hierarchical educational contexts. Ultimately, by empowering teachers as collaborative and adaptable professionals, this model of PLD offers new insights into enhancing the professional environments that shape teaching practice and young children’s learning.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Parent–school mobile communication in preschool: A qualitative study in Mexico
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: School-family communication in early childhood is increasingly mediated by mobile applications, yet important questions remain about what counts as high-quality content, how schools allocate topics between digital and face-to-face channels, and what costs these practices impose on teachers. This qualitative study examines how a mobile application shapes day-to-day parent-school communication in a Mexican preschool. Semi-structured interviews with four teachers and three mothers, combined with field observation, were thematically analyzed. The app supported timely and consistent exchanges about classroom life. Families valued brief, concrete descriptions of children’s socio-emotional participation, peer interactions, and strategies practiced, along with simple suggestions for follow-up at home. However, participants identified a depth gap when messages focused mainly on logistics, and teachers reported a workload tension between the burden of exhaustive daily reporting and the sense of security it provides to parents. A hybrid model of communication was preferred: routine updates and nonurgent questions were handled in the app, while complex, evaluative, or sensitive topics were addressed in planned one-to-one meetings. Reported short-term gains were primarily psychosocial, including higher trust and a closer working relationship between teachers and families. Findings support a shift from tool adoption to the quality of communicative practice in early childhood settings.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Promoting social skills and friendships in early childhood education: A case study of four children’s trajectories to inclusion
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: This paper reports on the changes reported on the social relations and skills of four children after the implementation of ProFriend (Promoting Friendship) in an early childhood education (ECE) setting. ProFriend is a programme developed considering the inclusive ECE principles by targeting all children’s access and participation and looking beyond imposed labels. The data of the study included friendship nominations, observations, children’s drawings, teachers’ interviews and research diary. The findings shed light on four children’s trajectories who faced challenges in forming friendships and whose individual characteristics (speech and language impairments and socio-emotional difficulties) were seen by teachers as barriers to their social development. The discussion focuses on how children’s exclusion can be minimised by enriching ECE curricula with some elements guiding teachers on how to approach the development of social skills and friendships in a meaningful and inclusive way.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: The impact of active transitions on preschool students’ self-regulation
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Early childhood education plays a pivotal role in fostering the holistic development of young learners through age-appropriate activities and interactions that support physical, social, emotional and cognitive growth. This study explored the relationship between active transitions in an early childhood education classroom and observable behaviour indicators of self-regulation in preschoolers, with a specific focus on the integration of yoga during transitional times. The objective was to investigate the impact of incorporating yoga on student self-regulation during large group literacy, as perceived by the preschool teacher. The research employed a collaborative action research design, engaging a preschool teacher in a reflective and systematic approach to improve classroom practices. Findings indicated that the integration of yoga, when including both challenging and sedentary poses, was associated with reductions in teacher-observed off-task behaviour during large group literacy, suggesting a possible positive influence on behaviour self-regulation. Results indicated that active transitions may support overall classroom management, increased instructional time and contributed to a comprehensive understanding of the effects of physical activity on young learners.

keyword_papers.title: AI intelligence within Teaching: A Multidimensional Evaluation of Large Language Model Education Agents in K-12 Education
keyword_papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are reshaping K–12 education by enabling adaptive and pedagogically responsive learning environments. This study presents a multidimensional evaluation of LLM-based learning agents using the Educational–Technical–Behavioural (ETB) Framework to assess pedagogical quality, technical reliability, and behavioural intelligence. ScienceSpark AI, a curriculum-aligned platform for the NSW Science 7–10 syllabus, was tested with Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 3, ChatGPT-5, and Claude Sonnet 4.5 within a unified agentic architecture. Using synthetic benchmarking, sandboxed simulations, and teacher-in-the-loop validation, the study found all models achieved strong curriculum alignment, factual accuracy, and multimodal feedback capability. Gemini 3 delivered the best technical performance, showing the lowest latency in conversation (~10s) and resource generation (~5.7s), while maintaining the high educational fidelity of Gemini 2.5 Pro. ChatGPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 excelled in conversational fluency and creative resource generation. Overall, the findings demonstrate that when grounded in transparent architecture and curriculum-driven design, LLM agents can provide both technical efficiency and equitable instructional support. The ETB Framework offers a replicable approach for evaluating and governing AI in education.

keyword_papers.title: A systematic literature review to implement large language model in higher education: issues and solutions
keyword_papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence-driven Chatbots, especially large language models (LLMs) like GPT-4, represent significant progress in digital education. These models excel in mimicking human-like text and transforming learning and teaching methods. This study examines the development, application, and impact of LLMs in education. It highlights their role in automating instructional tasks and promoting personalized learning experiences. Despite integration concerns and ethical debates, LLMs showcase the potential of AI to improve educational practices. Our research concludes that LLMs offer transformative opportunities for education. However, their incorporation requires careful ethical considerations, data privacy measures, and a balance between human educators and AI technologies. The findings suggest strategies for integrating LLMs into educational frameworks to enhance learning outcomes while preserving educational integrity.

keyword_papers.title: Embracing the Future of Medical Education With Large Language Model–Based Virtual Patients: Scoping Review
keyword_papers.abstract: Background In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have experienced rapid development. LLM-based virtual patients have begun to gain attention, offering new opportunities for simulations in medical education. Objective This study aims to systematically analyze the current applications, research trends, and challenges of LLM-based virtual patients in medical education and to explore potential future directions for development. Methods This study adheres to the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines. Five databases (Web of Science Core Collection, PubMed, IEEE Xplore, Embase, and Scopus) were searched from January 1, 2018, to June 24, 2025, to identify studies related to the application of LLM-based virtual patients in medical education. A comprehensive analysis of LLM-based virtual patients from research design to application and evaluation was conducted. Results A total of 28 studies were included in this scoping review. Analysis revealed that 92.9% (26/28) of the studies were published in the past 2 years, indicating that LLM-based virtual patient research is still in its early stages. The research primarily focuses on medical training and spans a wide range of medical disciplines. When using LLMs, advanced technologies such as social robots, virtual reality, and mixed reality are used to present LLM-based virtual patients. Combining these technologies with various supplementary tools enhances the realism of LLM-based virtual patients and improves user interaction. The evaluation of LLM-based virtual patients mainly emphasizes user experience. However, evaluation methods lack standardization, and only 13% (3/23) of studies used validated tools in assessing LLM-based virtual patients, while only 21.7% (5/23) of studies objectively measured learning outcomes facilitated by LLM-based virtual patients. All included studies expressed a positive attitude toward LLM-based virtual patients; however, they overlook privacy and security considerations in practical applications. Conclusions LLM-based virtual patients hold significant innovation potential in medical education and are still in the early stages of development. They are primarily applied in medical training and show promise in communication skills training, although they cannot replace real-world interactions. Moreover, the heterogeneity of research designs, the absence of nonverbal cues in interactions, and concerns regarding privacy and security limit their broader implementation. Future research should focus on improving the reliability, realism, safety, and scientific efficacy of LLM-based virtual patients. keyword_papers.title: Developing Effective Frameworks for Large Language Model–Based Medical Chatbots: Insights From Radiotherapy Education With ChatGPT
keyword_papers.abstract: This Viewpoint proposes a robust framework for developing a medical chatbot dedicated to radiotherapy education, emphasizing accuracy, reliability, privacy, ethics, and future innovations. By analyzing existing research, the framework evaluates chatbot performance and identifies challenges such as content accuracy, bias, and system integration. The findings highlight opportunities for advancements in natural language processing, personalized learning, and immersive technologies. When designed with a focus on ethical standards and reliability, large language model–based chatbots could significantly impact radiotherapy education and health care delivery, positioning them as valuable tools for future developments in medical education globally.

keyword_papers.title: Advancing AI in Higher Education: A Comparative Study of Large Language Model-Based Agents for Exam Question Generation, Improvement, and Evaluation
keyword_papers.abstract: The transformative capabilities of large language models (LLMs) are reshaping educational assessment and question design in higher education. This study proposes a systematic framework for leveraging LLMs to enhance question-centric tasks: aligning exam questions with course objectives, improving clarity and difficulty, and generating new items guided by learning goals. The research spans four university courses—two theory-focused and two application-focused—covering diverse cognitive levels according to Bloom’s taxonomy. A balanced dataset ensures representation of question categories and structures. Three LLM-based agents—VectorRAG, VectorGraphRAG, and a fine-tuned LLM—are developed and evaluated against a meta-evaluator, supervised by human experts, to assess alignment accuracy and explanation quality. Robust analytical methods, including mixed-effects modeling, yield actionable insights for integrating generative AI into university assessment processes. Beyond exam-specific applications, this methodology provides a foundational approach for the broader adoption of AI in post-secondary education, emphasizing fairness, contextual relevance, and collaboration. The findings offer a comprehensive framework for aligning AI-generated content with learning objectives, detailing effective integration strategies, and addressing challenges such as bias and contextual limitations. Overall, this work underscores the potential of generative AI to enhance educational assessment while identifying pathways for responsible implementation.

keyword_papers.title: Effectiveness of Robot-Mediated Learning in Fostering Children’s Social and Cognitive Development
keyword_papers.abstract: Engaging with social robots has been recognized as potentially beneficial for children facing social communication challenges, especially in developing skills such as joint attention. This systematic review examines the effectiveness of robot-mediated learning in enhancing children’s cognitive abilities, emotional resilience, and self-confidence, based on an analysis of research conducted between 2018 and 2025. While social robots show promise in delivering personalized and engaging educational experiences, challenges such as emotional dependence, accessibility, and ethical concerns persist. The review concludes that further research, particularly longitudinal studies and cross-cultural comparisons, is necessary to fully understand the long-term impacts of robot-mediated learning on children’s cognitive and social development. It explores the application of robotic technology in relation to children’s educational progress across different age groups. The review includes studies of various types, such as experimental, non-experimental, and research articles, covering diverse research fields, robots, contexts of use, target audiences, and outcomes. The findings highlight the growing potential of social robots to support children’s cognitive development by providing interactive and stimulating learning experiences. This review offers valuable insights for researchers and designers aiming to improve robotic interventions and tailor them to meet diverse developmental needs and educational settings.

keyword_papers.title: IMPACT OF TECHNOLOGY ON SOCIAL AND COGNITIVE DEVELOPMENT IN CHILDREN
keyword_papers.abstract:
Technology has inuenced children's social and cognitive development in recent years. This article explores both the
positive and negative impacts of technology on children's social and cognitive development. On the one hand, technology
can provide children with the opportunity to learn and engage in activities that may not be available in their home environment. This can lead to
increased condence and improved problem-solving skills. On the other hand, technology can lead to a decrease in physical activity, an increase in
feelings of isolation and loneliness, an over-dependence on technology, and a decrease in creativity and problem-solving skills. The article also
discusses technology's potential implications on children's social and cognitive development. It looks at how technology can both positively and
negatively affect children's development. It also looks at how it can be used to help them grow and develop healthily. Ultimately, this article
provides insight into the impact of technology on children's social and cognitive development and the potential implications of technology on
their lives

keyword_papers.title: Effects of Robotics Education on Young Children’s Cognitive Development: a Pilot Study with Eye-Tracking
keyword_papers.abstract: The emerging field of robotics education (RE) is a new and rapidly growing subject area worldwide. It may provide a playful and novel learning environment for children to engage with all aspects of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) learning. The purpose of this research is to examine how robotics learning activities may affect the cognitive abilities and cognitive processes of 6–8 years old children. The study adopted the mixed methods approach with a repeated measures design; three waves of data collection over 6 months, including quantitative data obtained from cognitive assessments and eye-tracking, and qualitative data from the interviews. A total of 31 children were recruited from an afterschool robotics program. To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first RE research that used a combination of eye-tracking, cognitive assessments, and interviews for examining the effect of RE on children. Using linear growth models, the results of cognitive assessments showed that children’s visuospatial working memory as well as logical and abstract reasoning skills improved over time. The interview data were analyzed by a thematic analysis. The results revealed that children perceived RE activities as game play, which made children more engaged in their study; parents found their children to be more focused on activities comparing to six months ago. Additionally, the visualization of the eye-tracking data suggested that children became more focused on RE activities and got faster to process the information across six months in general, which echoed the findings in assessments and interviews. Our findings may help educators and policymakers better understand the benefits of RE for young children.
keyword_papers.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology

keyword_papers.title: Digital Device Usage and Childhood Cognitive Development: Exploring Effects on Cognitive Abilities
keyword_papers.abstract: The increasing ubiquity of digital devices in childhood had outpaced the understanding of their effects on cognitive development, creating a significant research gap regarding their long-term impact. Objective: The present narrative overview explored the complex relationship between digital device usage and cognitive development in childhood. Methods: We conducted a comprehensive literature search across multiple databases, including PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science, to critically assess cognitive domains such as attention, memory, executive functions, problem-solving skills, and social cognition. Incorporating over 157 peer-reviewed studies published between 2001 and 2024, we used strict inclusion and exclusion criteria to ensure scientific rigor. Results: The review integrated empirical findings with established theoretical frameworks, particularly from cognitive development and media psychology, to highlight both the advantages and risks of early, frequent exposure to technology. The potential for digital devices to enhance cognitive skills, such as multitasking and information processing, was weighed against risks such as cognitive overload, diminished attention spans, and impaired social skills. We also examined psychological and behavioral outcomes, including identity formation, emotional regulation, and maladaptive behaviors associated with excessive screen time. Additionally, we identified strategies to mitigate negative effects, emphasizing structured digital engagement and parental involvement to support healthy cognitive and psychological growth. Our findings provided actionable recommendations for parents, educators, and policymakers, promoting optimal digital practices that enhanced cognitive development while safeguarding against potential harms. Conclusions: The review offered essential insights for stakeholders in child development, education, and policy-making, highlighting the need for balanced integration of digital tools in childhood learning environments.

keyword_papers.title: Usefulness of interactive video-based instruction on learning performance in relation to cognitive development of children with moderate intellectual disability
keyword_papers.abstract: The usefulness of information and communication technology has been witnessed around the globe with the occurrence of rapid changes in the field of education i.e. through the formal or informal way. For this, the researchers have assessed Interactive video-based instruction (IVBI) on (N = 95; males = 47 & females = 48 age range between 12 and 15 years) moderate intellectual disability children in Guwahati, Assam, India from three day-care rehabilitation centres. The main objective was to examine the effect of IVBI intervention (IIVBI & CIVBI) on academic performance in association with the cognitive development of children with moderate intellectual disability in a comfortable setting within working hours. The findings conclude that children in the CIVBI group performed more actively as compared to IIVBI and comparison group, and it was due to the involvement of video-based instruction that helped understand the topic more precisely and acts effectively for CIVBI children in an experimental setting.
